# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

6	# Subagent-Driven Development
7

10	**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. The only reasons to stop are: BLOCKED status you cannot resolve, ambiguity that genuinely prevents progress, or all tasks complete. "Should I continue?" prompts and progress summaries waste their time — they asked you to execute the plan, so execute it.

119	## Setup
120	
121	Ensure the work happens in an isolated workspace: use
122	hyperpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one.
123	Never start implementation on a main/master branch without your human
124	partner's explicit consent.
125	
126	Conversation memory does not survive compaction. In real sessions,
127	controllers that lost their place have re-dispatched entire completed task
128	sequences — the single most expensive failure observed. Track progress in
129	a ledger file, not only in todos.
130	
131	- Each plan owns a workspace: at skill start, run this skill's
132	  `scripts/sdd-dir PLAN_FILE` — it prints the plan's scratch directory
133	  under the user cache
134	  (`${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-~/.cache}/hyperpowers/sdd/<per-repo-key>/plans/<plan-slug>-<hash8>/`),
135	  home to every artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, reports, review
136	  packages, tier-skip summary. The cache is off any protected path, so
137	  writing there never triggers a permission prompt, and it is outside the
138	  working tree, so it can never be committed. Another plan's directory is
139	  never yours to read or write.
140	- Check for this plan's ledger at `<workspace>/progress.md` — this plan's
141	  workspace only, never a sibling's. The workspace is the plan's identity:
142	  `scripts/sdd-dir` maps a plan to ONE directory whatever path form you
143	  hand it, so a ledger sitting in YOUR workspace is this plan's progress
144	  even when its first line records the path in another form (relative vs
145	  absolute, or through a symlink). Resolve that line and compare the file
146	  it points to, not the string. Tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are
147	  DONE — do not re-dispatch them; resume at the first task without one. A
148	  task whose last line is a fix round is mid-loop: resume the loop at the
149	  next round. A task whose last line is its implementer identity is a
150	  dispatch in flight: do not re-dispatch — reconcile that agent first
151	  (list your live children, chase its report), resume it by the recorded
152	  id where your harness allows, and only if it cannot be recovered
153	  dispatch a takeover, recording the takeover's identity beside the
154	  original. A first line that resolves to a genuinely different plan
155	  file means this workspace is corrupt, not that you wandered into a
156	  sibling's: stop and surface it to your human partner rather than
157	  starting fresh on top of another plan's state.
158	- Create the ledger with its identity as the first line:
159	  `# SDD ledger — plan: <plan file path>`.
160	- The ledger is your recovery map: the commits it names exist in git even
161	  when your context no longer remembers creating them. After compaction,
162	  trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
163	- The workspace is scratch, not a deliverable. The Finish step deletes it
164	  once the final whole-branch review is clean; `scripts/sdd-dir` also
165	  reclaims sibling workspaces idle for 14+ days as a backstop for sessions
166	  that never reach Finish. It never reclaims the workspace you are using —
167	  every call refreshes it — so a resumed session always finds its ledger.
168	
169	Read the plan once, note its context and Global Constraints, and create a
170	todo per task where your harness surfaces todos — the ledger is the
171	progress record either way; todos mirror it, never replace it. Read the
172	plan's `**Spec:**` header and the spec file it names: the spec is the
173	binding authority the plan argues from, and conflicts inside the plan
174	resolve against it. A plan whose spec is `none` or unreachable gets a
175	ledger line saying so — without a spec, a conflict has no tiebreaker but
176	your human partner.
177	
178	Before dispatching Task 1, scan the plan once for conflicts, writing down
179	what you checked as you check it:
180	
181	- tasks that contradict each other or the plan's Global Constraints
182	- anything the plan explicitly mandates that the review rubric treats as a
183	  defect (a test that asserts nothing, verbatim duplication of a logic block)
184	
185	The scan's output is a table, not a verdict. One row for every pair of tasks
186	that share a file or an interface: the two tasks, what one produces against
187	what the other consumes, and what you found. One row for every task: whether
188	its own text agrees with itself — the tests it specifies against the code it
189	specifies, the files it creates against the files it later touches. "The scan
190	is clean" without those rows is not a scan you ran.
191	
192	Write the table to the ledger. Then present everything it surfaced to your
193	human partner as ONE batched question — each finding beside the plan text
194	that mandates it, asking which governs — before execution begins, not one
195	interrupt per discovery mid-plan. Each finding is a decision with
196	consequences downstream, so it gets the shape the brainstorming skill's
197	Deciding Together section describes: the conflict and what each resolution
198	costs in chat, then the selection widget to collect the answers. If the scan
199	is clean, proceed without comment. The review loop remains the net for
200	conflicts that only emerge from implementation.
201	
202	## Model Selection
203	
204	Match the model to the task's difficulty rather than defaulting. Two rules are
205	defaults you will get wrong by omission, so they stay here: **always specify
206	the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent** — an omitted model inherits
207	your session's, usually the most capable and most expensive — and **a mid-tier
208	model is the floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose
209	descriptions**, whatever the schedule pressure. The cheapest tier is for
210	transcription, where the task's own text carries the complete code to write,
211	and for single-file mechanical fixes. The per-role guidance, the complexity
212	signals, and the fix-loop escalation rule are in
213	[model-selection.md](model-selection.md).
214	
215	## The Task Loop
216	
217	**Batch small same-shape work.** When the plan lists several tasks that are
218	each a small, independent edit of the same kind — the same one-line fix,
219	constant change, or field addition repeated across files — do not dispatch
220	one subagent per task. Compose ONE dispatch brief listing every file and
221	its change, send the whole batch to a single subagent, and review its diff
222	as one unit. Reserve one-dispatch-per-task for work that needs its own
223	judgment, its own tests, or its own review surface.
224	A batch's effective risk tier for the per-task Codex gate is the MAX of the
225	batched tasks' declared tiers — batching low-tier tasks never manufactures
226	a gate skip.
227	
228	Everything you paste into a dispatch prompt — and everything a subagent
229	prints back — stays resident in your context for the rest of the session
230	and is re-read on every later turn. Hand artifacts over as files.
231	
232	**Waiting on dispatched subagents:** never poll a wait interface with
233	short timeouts, and never sit in one silent, open-ended wait either.
234	While you have local work — ledger updates, packaging the next review,
235	reading reports — keep working; child results arrive on their own.
236	When you are genuinely idle, wait in bounded stretches (five to ten
237	minutes, where your platform allows), and between stretches post one
238	line of status and reconcile your live children: list them, and chase
239	any that finished without reporting. A bounded stretch keeps nearly
240	all of a long wait's efficiency while guaranteeing a stuck or lost
241	child is noticed within minutes, not at the end of the session.
242	
243	### 1. Dispatch the implementer
244	
245	Record BASE (`git rev-parse HEAD`) before dispatching — the review package
246	and fix-round diffs need it.
247	
248	- **Task brief:** before dispatching an implementer, run this skill's
249	  `scripts/task-brief PLAN_FILE N` — it extracts the task's full text to a
250	  uniquely named file and prints `wrote <path>: <N> lines`. Take the path
251	  from that line; do not paste the line itself into a dispatch. Compose the
252	  dispatch so the
253	  brief stays the single source of
254	  requirements. Your dispatch should contain: (1) one line on where this
255	  task fits in the project; (2) the brief path, introduced as "read this
256	  first — it is your requirements, with the exact values to use verbatim";
257	  (3) interfaces and decisions from earlier tasks that the brief cannot
258	  know; (4) your resolution of any ambiguity you noticed in the brief;
259	  (5) the report-file path and report contract. Exact values (numbers,
260	  magic strings, signatures, test cases) appear only in the brief. Never
261	  make a subagent read the whole plan file.
262	- **Report file:** name the implementer's report file after the brief
263	  (brief `…/task-N-brief.md` → report `…/task-N-report.md`) and put it in
264	  the dispatch prompt. The implementer writes the full report there and
265	  returns only status, commits, a one-line test summary, and concerns.
266	- A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history. Do not
267	  paste accumulated prior-task summaries ("state after Tasks 1-3") into
268	  later dispatches — a real session's dispatch hit 42k chars of which 99%
269	  was pasted history. A fresh subagent needs its task, the interfaces it
270	  touches, and the global constraints. Nothing else.
271	- The dispatch carries the no-subagents contract (it is in the
272	  implementer template): the implementer never dispatches subagents —
273	  not helpers, and never a reviewer. Review arrives from you, after the
274	  report. In real sessions, every reviewer a worker spawned duplicated
275	  the task review the controller dispatched anyway — a full extra
276	  review seat per task.
277	- Subagents follow hyperpowers:test-driven-development for the task's tests.
278	- If an earlier task deferred a finding in the area this task touches — a
279	  Minor in the ledger, or one your human partner decided — carry a pointer
280	  to that ledger entry in the dispatch.
281	- Record the implementer's agent identity from the dispatch result in the
282	  ledger's task entry (`Task <N>: implementer <agent-id-or-name>`) —
283	  fix-loop rounds 1-3 resume this agent, and after compaction the ledger is
284	  the only place the identity survives once its agent has exited. An
285	  identity that was never written down forces a fresh takeover where a
286	  resume was owed.
287	- Never dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts).
288	
289	Template: [implementer-prompt.md](implementer-prompt.md)
290	
291	### 2. Handle the report
292	
293	**Subagent Reports Are Claims.** Subagent reports are claims, not
294	evidence. Before acting on any completed-status report (DONE or DONE_WITH_CONCERNS) or a fix report —
295	dispatching the reviewer, re-running a gate, marking a task complete — the
296	controller re-runs the named covering test command directly and compares
297	the output against the report. A misreported result is a failed task:
298	re-dispatch with the discrepancy named, not a bookkeeping correction.
299	
300	Every implementer and fix dispatch names either its covering test
301	command(s) or an explicit `no covering command: <rationale>` line plus the
302	controller's substitute verification (read the diff against the brief;
303	render or grep the changed doc). A dispatch naming neither is malformed —
304	fix the dispatch, not the rule.
305	
306	A covering command must be able to fail. One that can no-op on the state
307	under test — a changed-files linter on a clean tree, a test filter that
308	matches nothing — is not covering evidence, however honestly it exits 0.
309	Name the files or the test ids explicitly so the command exercises what
310	the report claims.
311	
312	Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:
313	
314	**DONE:** Generate the review package (`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD`, from this skill's directory — it prints `wrote <path>: <N> commit(s), <N> bytes`, so take the path from that line; BASE is the commit you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task). If `review-package` exits non-zero, read its stderr and fix the range before dispatching — exit 2 means bad inputs (wrong argument count, a missing plan file, a ref that does not resolve) or an ancestry check git itself could not answer (a missing or corrupt object); exit 3 means BASE..HEAD is empty or HEAD is not a descendant of BASE, usually a wrong-branch commit; never dispatch a reviewer without a package. Otherwise, dispatch the task reviewer with the path.
315	
316	**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.
317	
318	**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.
319	
320	**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
321	1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
322	2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
323	3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
324	4. If the plan itself is wrong, stop and escalate to your human partner — the plan text, what it breaks, and the correction you would make
325	
326	**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.
327	
328	If the implementer asks questions — before starting or mid-task — answer
329	clearly and completely, provide additional context if needed, and don't
330	rush it into implementation.
331	
332	### 3. Review the task
333	
334	Per-task reviews are task-scoped gates. The broad review happens once, at the
335	final whole-branch review. Never skip the task review, and never accept a
336	report missing either verdict — spec compliance AND task quality are both
337	required. Implementer self-review never replaces the task review; both are
338	needed. Note the task's effective risk tier as you go (see Risk Tiers,
339	below) — the Claude task review always runs, but the tier decides whether
340	step 4's per-task Codex gate does.
341	
342	- Hand the reviewer its diff as a file: run this skill's
343	  `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD` — it prints
344	  `wrote <path>: <N> commit(s), <N> bytes`, so take the path from that line
345	  and pass it to the reviewer (or, without bash: `git log --oneline`,
346	  `git diff --stat`, and `git diff -U10` for the range, redirected to one
347	  uniquely named file). The output never enters your own context, and the reviewer sees
348	  the commit list, stat summary, and full diff with context in one Read
349	  call. Use the BASE you recorded before dispatching the implementer —
350	  never `HEAD~1`, which silently truncates multi-commit tasks. Never
351	  dispatch a task reviewer without a diff file.
352	- **Reviewer inputs:** the task reviewer gets three paths — the same brief
353	  file, the report file, and the review package — plus the global
354	  constraints that bind the task. Write those global constraints to a small
355	  file alongside the brief and report: the per-task Codex gate takes the
356	  same file as its global-constraints handoff.
357	- The global-constraints block you hand the reviewer is its attention
358	  lens. Copy the binding requirements verbatim from the plan's Global
359	  Constraints section or the spec: exact values, exact formats, and the
360	  stated relationships between components ("same layout as X", "matches
361	  Y"). The reviewer's template already carries the process rules (YAGNI,
362	  test hygiene, review method) — the constraints block is for what THIS
363	  project's spec demands.
364	- Do not add open-ended directives like "check all uses" or "run race tests
365	  if useful" without a concrete, task-specific reason
366	- Do not ask a reviewer to re-run tests the implementer already ran on the
367	  same code — the implementer's report carries the test evidence
368	- Do not pre-judge findings for the reviewer — never instruct a reviewer to
369	  ignore or not flag a specific issue. If you believe a finding would be a
370	  false positive, let the reviewer raise it and adjudicate it in the review
371	  loop. If the prompt you are writing contains "do not flag," "don't treat X
372	  as a defect," "at most Minor," or "the plan chose" — stop: you are
373	  pre-judging, usually to spare yourself a review loop. When the plan supplies
374	  example code, weaknesses in that code are fair review targets — the example
375	  was a starting point, not evidence that its weaknesses were chosen.
376	The task reviewer may report "⚠️ Cannot verify from diff" items — requirements
377	that live in unchanged code or span tasks. These do not block the rest of the
378	review, but you must resolve each one yourself before marking the task
379	complete: you hold the plan and cross-task context the reviewer
380	lacks. If you confirm an item is a real gap, treat it as a failed spec
381	review — it enters the fix loop with the other findings.
382	
383	Template: [task-reviewer-prompt.md](task-reviewer-prompt.md)
384	
385	### 4. The fix loop
386	
387	The loop triggers when the review reports spec ❌, any Critical or Important
388	finding, a ⚠️ item you confirmed as a real gap, or a blocking finding from
389	the per-task Codex gate below.
390	
391	Task-reviewer findings are claims too. The resumed implementer verifies
392	each finding against the code before fixing it
393	(hyperpowers:receiving-code-review); a finding is declined only as
394	refuted or corrected with file:line evidence, which the controller
395	records in the ledger; a confirmed finding is fixed or carried open; a
396	finding nobody can settle stays open and counts against the round cap.
397	
398	Before the loop starts, two routes leave it immediately:
399	
400	- Record Minor findings in the progress ledger as you go
401	  (`Task <N>: minor (deferred): <one-liner>`), and point the final
402	  whole-branch review at that list so it can triage which must be fixed
403	  before merge. A roll-up nobody reads is a silent discard. Minor findings
404	  never enter the loop.
405	- A finding labeled plan-mandated — or any finding that conflicts with what
406	  the plan's text requires — is your human partner's decision: present the
407	  finding and the plan text beside it and ask which governs. Do not dismiss
408	  the finding because the plan mandates it, and do not dispatch a fix that
409	  contradicts the plan without asking.
410	
411	Everything else enters the loop — the Claude task reviewer's blocking
412	findings and the per-task Codex gate's blocking findings alike. They are ONE
413	loop with ONE shared cap of **five rounds per task**: the gate does not run
414	a count of its own. A fix round is one fix dispatch — or one
415	controller-applied de-minimis fix — plus one scoped re-review.
416	
417	**Rounds 1-3 — resume the original implementer.** Send it the open findings
418	verbatim. Its context is intact: it knows the task, the code, and its own
419	choices. If your harness cannot send another message to a live subagent,
420	dispatch a fresh implementer carrying the brief path, the report-file path,
421	and the findings — the report file is the persistent memory either way.
422	
423	**Rounds 4-5 — dispatch a fresh takeover implementer on a more capable
424	model** (per Model Selection), with the brief path, the report-file path,
425	the open findings, and this framing: "A prior implementer attempted this
426	task [N] times; you own it now. Read the report file for what was tried." A
427	loop that survives three resumes usually means the implementer cannot see
428	its own problem — fresh eyes and a capability bump in one move.
429	
430	**Every round, either way:** the implementer fixes, re-runs the tests
431	covering the amended code, appends its fix report to the same report file,
432	and returns the short contract. Before re-dispatching the reviewer, confirm
433	the fix report contains the covering tests, the command run, and the
434	output; dispatch the re-review once all three are present. That
435	precondition covers the findings the round fixed; a round that declines
436	every finding is defined below. Name the covering test files in the fix
437	message — a one-line fix does not need the whole suite. The per-task loop
438	resumes an implementer rather than dispatching a fixer, so it never uses
439	[fix-subagent-prompt.md](fix-subagent-prompt.md) — that template belongs to
440	the final review's one fix wave.
441	
442	**The re-review is scoped.** Run `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD`
443	where FIX_BASE is the head the previous review saw, and dispatch
444	[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md) with the findings list, the
445	brief, the report file, and the printed diff path. The re-reviewer verdicts
446	each finding ADDRESSED, NOT ADDRESSED, or DECLINED — a refuted or corrected
447	finding whose file:line evidence the re-reviewer has confirmed; an unconfirmed
448	decline stays NOT ADDRESSED — and flags new breakage in the fix diff only. The
449	controller records each DECLINED finding in the ledger with its evidence. New
450	Critical/Important breakage in the fix diff joins the open findings list.
451	Out-of-scope observations go to the ledger as deferred minors — they never
452	extend the loop. Every round in this loop ends with the scoped re-review —
453	never a full task-reviewer re-run, whatever the finding's origin.
454	
455	**A round that declines every finding changes no code.** There is no fix
456	diff and no covering test to confirm; the implementer's report is the
457	artifact, carrying for each finding the refuted or corrected evidence at
458	file:line. Skip `scripts/review-package` for that round — its range is
459	empty — and dispatch the scoped re-review with the findings list, the brief,
460	the report, and the previous review's package path, so the re-reviewer
461	verdicts each finding DECLINED or NOT ADDRESSED from the evidence alone. The
462	covering-tests precondition applies only to findings that were fixed. Record
463	the round as `(0 addressed, <Y> declined, <Z> open)`; a NOT ADDRESSED verdict
464	keeps that finding open and the round counts toward the cap as usual.
465	
466	**After each round,** append to the ledger:
467	`Task <N>: fix round <R>/5 (<X> addressed, <Y> declined, <Z> open — <finding one-liners>; commits <a7>..<b7>)`
468	
469	Never fix findings yourself in the controller session — your context stays
470	clean for coordination, and controller fixes skip review. One narrow
471	exception: a fix fully specified by the finding itself — exact file, exact
472	lines, exact replacement, no judgment left — touching at most 3 lines in
473	one file with no new logic, may be controller-applied — one finding per
474	reach; a round holding two such findings is not de minimis. The exception
475	waives nothing else: it consumes a fix round and ends in the same scoped
476	re-review; the controller applies the edit and runs the fix's covering
477	command FIRST — a failure means the fix was not de minimis: revert the
478	edit, spend no round, and go back to the round's own rule — then commits
479	the verified fix (the re-review packages committed diffs — an
480	uncommitted fix hands it nothing) and appends the fix report — the
481	command, its output, and a diff summary — to the task's report file
482	itself, exactly as an implementer would. Its ledger line keeps the
483	fix-round schema with the marker inside it:
484	`Task <N>: fix round <R>/5 controller-applied (de minimis) (<X> addressed, <Y> declined, <Z> open — <finding one-liners>; commits <a7>..<b7>)`.
485	Reaching for it twice in the same task means the findings are not de
486	minimis — go back to the round's own rule: resume the implementer at
487	rounds 1-3, dispatch the takeover at rounds 4-5.
488	
489	**Codex Review Gate (Claude Code only).** When running under Claude Code, add
490	a Codex **code** review gate at two points — here, per task, and once more
491	at the final whole-branch review — following
492	[../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md](../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md).
493	Probe once per skill run and reuse the result; if Codex is absent, emit the
494	no-Codex notice once and run both gates as no-ops.
495	
496	- **Per task:** after the task reviewer approves (spec ✅ and quality approved) and
497	  before marking the task complete, run the gate (standard/high effective tiers; an effective-low task skips it per Risk Tiers below, recording the tier-skip event instead) using the per-task code recipe
498	  with `--base <the task BASE you recorded before dispatching the implementer>`.
499	  Provide the task brief path, implementer report path, review-package path, and
500	  the global-constraints file you wrote in step 3. The gate's dossier `--adjudications` inputs carry the plan's `**Spec:**` file path beside any spec-gate ledger, so the reviewer is handed the binding authority instead of inferring it.
501	- **Rounds are shared, not stacked.** Blocking findings from this gate enter
502	  the same five-round loop above, at the next round number — the gate has no
503	  separate Codex ceiling of its own. The task's fix-round budget is five,
504	  shared across Claude-reviewer rounds and Codex-gate rounds. Three mechanics
505	  keep that single budget honest:
506	
507	  1. **One `GATE_DIR` for this task's whole gate lifecycle.** Create it at
508	     the task's first gate invocation and reuse that same dir for every
509	     Codex re-round of this task — the gate doc's §3 contract, "Use one
510	     `GATE_DIR` for the whole gate." `gate-round`'s counter lives in that
511	     dir, so it counts exactly this task's gate rounds and nothing else.
512	     When the `GATE_DIR` is first created, record it in the progress ledger
513	     as one line `Task N gate dir: <path>`; on resume (or any later Codex
514	     re-round), reuse the ledgered path instead of creating a new one; if
515	     the ledgered dir no longer exists (cache purged), treat the task's
516	     prior gate rounds as unknown and fail closed: do not assume zero —
517	     reconstruct the consumed-round count from the ledger's fix-round
518	     entries and, if gate rounds cannot be established, surface via BLOCKED
519	     rather than restarting the count.
520	  2. **Let the counter do the arithmetic.** `gate-round` compares its LOCAL
521	     count — gate rounds only, monotonic within the `GATE_DIR` — against a
522	     ceiling, so the ceiling must leave gate rounds out; they are already in
523	     that count. Pass `--consumed <NON-gate fix rounds this task has consumed
524	     so far>` (all fix/re-review rounds, whatever the finding's origin — the
525	     gate's own invocation rounds are excluded only because `gate-round`'s
526	     counter already holds them) and the script derives the ceiling from the
527	     shared five-round cap itself. Recompute the consumed count at each call:
528	     non-gate rounds may land between gate rounds. Do not hand-compute
529	     `--ceiling` for a task gate — that is how twenty measured task gates
530	     recorded ceilings of 1, 2, 6, and 7, two of which the cap makes
531	     impossible. `--consumed` cannot express them.
532	  3. **A spent cap is BLOCKED, not a gate round.** When the task's consumed
533	     rounds already total five, `--consumed 5` yields a ceiling of zero and
534	     the gate backstops on its first call. That is the fail-closed floor, not
535	     the intended path: check before calling, and when the cap is spent follow
536	     the breaker below and surface the task as BLOCKED rather than spending a
537	     gate invocation to learn it.
538	
539	  The invariant in one line: **local gate rounds + non-gate fix rounds ≤ 5**,
540	  enforced because `gate-round` blocks (verdict `backstop`) the moment its
541	  local count would exceed the ceiling. Count every round the
542	  gate runs against the task's shared budget — each gate round consumes one
543	  of the five, exactly like a reviewer round. After a Codex-triggered fix,
544	  the scoped re-review verifies it; the gate re-runs only once that
545	  re-review verdicts every finding ADDRESSED or DECLINED.
546	
547	**The breaker.** When round 5's re-review — or a per-task Codex gate at the
548	spent cap — still leaves blocking findings open, stop dispatching. The task
549	does not silently continue and nothing is parked on your own authority:
550	surface the open findings to your human partner as BLOCKED, each with the
551	rounds already spent, what was tried, and the evidence. Ledger it:
552	`Task <N>: BLOCKED at cap — <finding one-liners>`. They decide what happens
553	next.
554	
555	### 5. Complete the task
556	
557	When the review comes back clean — the task reviewer approved, every
558	fix-loop finding is addressed or declined, and the per-task Codex gate
559	approved or was skipped by tier — append the completion line to the ledger
560	in the same message as your other bookkeeping:
561	
562	- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, review clean)`
563	
564	Then mark the task's todo complete, where you keep todos, and move on.
565	Never move to the next task while the review has open Critical/Important
566	issues.
567	
568	## Risk Tiers (per-task Codex gate applicability)
569	
570	Tiers are `low`, `standard`, `high`, declared per task in the plan. A task
571	skips the per-task Codex gate only when all three hold: declared low, the
572	plan's own Codex gate actually reviewed the plan, and no escalation trigger
573	fired at any point during execution. That skip is recorded durably. An
574	unreviewed low tier — plan gate skipped, degraded, or outcome unknown —
575	executes as standard, and a task demoted that way runs the full train and
576	records NO tier-skip event. The Claude task reviewer and the final
577	whole-branch train never tier off. When any task did skip, write
578	`tier-skips.md` in this plan's workspace; Final Review hands its path to the
579	final reviewer and the final Codex gate. The escalation triggers, the
580	fallback rules, and the exact ledger line shape are in
581	[risk-tiers.md](risk-tiers.md) — read it before dispatching any task declared
582	low.
583	
584	## Final Review
585	
586	The final whole-branch review gets a package too: run
587	`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD` (MERGE_BASE = the commit the
588	branch started from, e.g. `git merge-base main HEAD`) — take the path from the
589	`wrote <path>: ...` line and include it in the final review dispatch, so the
590	final reviewer reads one file instead of re-deriving the branch diff with git
591	commands. Dispatch
592	on the most capable available model (see Model Selection), using
593	hyperpowers:requesting-code-review's
594	[code-reviewer.md](../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md). Point it at
595	the ledger's deferred-minor lines — and at `tier-skips.md`, if any task
596	skipped its per-task gate — so it can triage which must be fixed before
597	merge.
598	
599	If the final whole-branch review returns findings, dispatch ONE fix subagent
600	with the complete findings list — not one fixer per finding. Compose the
601	dispatch from [fix-subagent-prompt.md](fix-subagent-prompt.md).
602	Per-finding fixers each rebuild context and re-run suites; a real
603	session's final-review fix wave cost more than all its tasks combined.
604	Then run exactly one scoped re-review of the fix wave
605	(`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD` over the fix range,
606	[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md) using its Final-wave usage note).
607	There is no second fix wave: anything the re-review leaves open — and any
608	finding that conflicts with the plan's text — goes to your human partner
609	with the evidence, as BLOCKED, when finishing-a-development-branch presents
610	the options.
611	
612	**Codex Review Gate — final whole-branch (Claude Code only).** After the final code-reviewer
613	subagent and its fix wave, and before hyperpowers:finishing-a-development-branch,
614	run the gate using the final whole-branch code recipe with `--base <branch
615	merge-base, e.g. git merge-base main HEAD>`. Provide the branch
616	review-package path, plan or requirements path, the Minor findings ledger if
617	present, and the tier-skip summary if any task skipped. The final dossier passes the plan's `**Spec:**` file as a `--doc` input beside the plan, and carries the tier-skip summary among its `--adjudications`. Resolve blocking
618	findings with one fix subagent carrying the complete list, per this
619	section's existing guidance, before finishing. After any Codex-triggered
620	final-review fix, re-run the final code-reviewer before re-running the final
621	Codex gate.
622	
623	Unlike the per-task gate, the final gate keeps a ceiling of its own: the
624	gate's convergence stop-rule and per-gate backstop bound this loop (code
625	gates use a code-gate backstop of 3 rounds). If the backstop is hit with
626	unresolved blocking findings, surface them to your human partner rather than
627	looping.
628	
629	## Finish
630	
631	When the final whole-branch review is clean and its fixes are merged:
632	
633	1. **Delete this plan's workspace** with `rm -rf <workspace>` (the path
634	   `scripts/sdd-dir <plan>` prints — the directory holding this plan's
635	   ledger, briefs, reports, review packages, and tier-skip summary).
636	2. **Verify deletion** with `test ! -d "<workspace>"` to confirm it is gone.
637	
638	A clean finish that leaves the workspace behind is an INCOMPLETE finish —
639	"keeping it for reference" is not an option; the repo's commits are the
640	durable record. Sibling directories belong to other plans; leave them
641	alone. The 14-day reclaim in `scripts/sdd-dir` is only the backstop for
642	sessions that never got here.
643	
644	Use hyperpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.
645	
646	## Common Rationalizations
647	
648	The excuses that show up mid-run and what is actually true:
649	[common-rationalizations.md](common-rationalizations.md). Read it the moment you
650	catch yourself justifying a shortcut.
651	
652	## Example Workflow
653	
654	A complete worked run, dispatch through finish:
655	[example-workflow.md](example-workflow.md).
656
